messages.subject: Flow centrality of hemibrain neurons
parts:
Not sure if this is the best place to post it but I have a question on hemibrain neurons...

Segregation indices for most of the hemibrain neurons seem (not surprisingly) rather low that I would guess calculating flow centrality wouldn't work in classifying axons or dendrites (or input-specific zones vs. out-specific zones)? 0.5 - 0.6 should already be a modest mixing of inputs and outputs, and most neuron seem much lower than that. Did I miss something here? Or is it that, empirically, using flow centrality just works well? 

Best,

Zhihao

messages.author: 7f0257cd1389289f
messages.subject: Re: [nat-user] Flow centrality of hemibrain neurons
parts:
Dear Zhihao,

I think you should get some specific input from Alex Bates on this, but essentially you will not be able to use flow centrality thresholds that you are used to in FAFB with hemibrain data. As far as I can tell the general reason for this is that many hemibrain neurons have 

Most of their axonal output synapses
Most of the inputs onto those axonal arbours (many inputs can be on the shaft or very close to the shaft and are therefore well-recovered).

But proportionally fewer dendritic inputs (mean of ~25% across the brain) and presumably dendritic outputs.

This differential synapse recovery rate will skew some analytics including flow centrality. Of course there will also be some neurons that are truncated etc.

But this does not meant that you can't use flow centrality at all. You just may need to recalibrate.

All the best,

Greg.

messages.subject: Re: [nat-user] Flow centrality of hemibrain neurons
parts:
Thanks for the explanation Greg and Alex!

Did I read it right that you estimate only ~25% of dendritic synapses are recovered? It’s possible that this is good enough for asserting most connections at the neuron-to-neuron level (given distributed synapses, Schneider-Mizell et al. 2016) and, with the "right" percentage of axons and dendrites, I could imagine 25% be buried as the dendrite part of the reported 0.8, 0.9 precision/recall (attached screenshot from Scheffer et al. 2020). It still seems low and will disproportionately affect interpretation of number of synapses between a given pair of neurons in the dataset (depending on how much of the connection is made up by axon-axonic synapses or by axon-dendritic synapses).

Best,

Zhihao


On Jun 13, 2020, at 4:47 PM, Alexander Bates <aba...@mrc-lmb.cam.ac.uk> wrote:

Hey!

I agree with Greg. Empirically, we find that for complete neurons with the soma rooted correctly, the algorithm performs well, produces the same splits in FAFB (even if segregation score is different) and, in the few cases where I have looked, the split fits our impression based on the 3D morphology (thicker axons, with boutons).

I am not sure how it compares with the electronic method Lou and Stephen have been using, but as far as I can see, the only ‘mistakes’ (judged intuitively) being made, happen when a neuron is not well skeletonized or is missing parts.

Segregation scores will not be directly comparable, FAFB - hemibrain.

Best,

Alex
